title: Prompt-chaining cost probes & rough experiments
content:
Purpose / quick note to self:
- sketch lightweight experiments to quantify per-request token cost and latency when using multi-step prompt chains vs single-shot prompts for structured extraction and multi-turn planning.
- surface how Redwood's prefix/KV cache and batching interact with common chaining patterns (e.g., plan -> execute -> verify).

TL;DR hypotheses (what I expect):
1) multi-step chains often increase total tokens but can reduce hallucination and improve pass rates on structured tasks (higher P@k).
2) if intermediate steps reuse large shared prefixes across users/requests, caching reduces incremental cost; otherwise chains multiply context cost.
3) batching + non-blocking execution may amortize overhead, but SLOs (tail latency) get worse for long chains unless we pipeline.

Papers / short reads I'm referencing:
- "Self-Consistency and Chain-of-Thought" (notes to compare single-shot vs chain-of-thought sampling) -> arxiv:2203.02155 (placeholder: compare multi-sample cost)
- Blog: "When to chain prompts" (internal link in Confluence) -> paraphrase: chaining helps complex reasoning but increases token volume.
- Related OSS: few-shot templates in docs / examples in repo playground (see linked issue).

Concrete experiments (minimal reproducible):
A) Structured-extraction baseline (single-shot):
  - Task: extract JSON fields from 3-paragraph product description (10k samples synthetic).
  - Prompt: instruction + 5-shot example -> single call.
  - Measure: tokens in, tokens out, latency p50/p95/p99, extraction precision/recall, cost per 1k requests.

B) Two-step chain (plan then extract):
  - Step 1: plan/outline -> short plan (20-80 tokens).
  - Step 2: extract using plan as additional prompt context.
  - Measure same metrics + incremental prefix reuse (does plan appear in cache across requests?).

C) Three-step (plan -> generate candidate values -> verify):
  - Step 2 sample n=3 candidates, Step 3 verify + choose best.
  - Measure blowup in total tokens with sampling; compute cost vs gain in quality.

Experiment design notes:
- Keep model fixed (choose small/med/large family: e.g., redwood-v1-small / medium / large) to isolate prompt pattern effects.
- Use same batching policy initially (no special pipelining). Then run a pass with pipeline enabled to see latency improvement.
- For caching: run two regimes: (1) all prompts randomized so prefixes don't match, (2) templates & shared instruction text constant so caching helps.
- Track per-route console metrics: token breakdown, cache hit rate, per-step latency.

Hypothetical cost math (rough):
- Single-shot: avg tokens in 420 + tokens out 60 = 480 tokens per request.
- Two-step: step1 60 tokens in/out + step2 420+60 = 540 total -> ~12% token increase. If cache hits on the big 420 prefix, effective additional incremental tokens can be small (e.g., only 60+60).
- 3-step sampling n=3: tokens multiply by ~3 for sampling stage -> heavy cost (2–4x). Need to quantify when quality gain justifies.

Operational considerations for Redwood features:
- Prefix/KV cache: important to test with different cache TTLs and shard affinities. If plan text is unique per request, cache brings little benefit. If instruction templates are stable, cache reduces marginal token cost dramatically.
- Batching: long chains create more small calls; need to evaluate batching windows vs latency SLOs. Continuous batching might help when throughput is high.
- Model routing fallback: when dedicated pool saturates, fallbacks to smaller model could be cheaper but change hallucination profile — integrate into chain gracefully (e.g., verify step runs on larger model only).

Checklist for running the sweep:
- [ ] Build synthetic dataset: 10k product descriptions with controlled noise (swap adjectives, add irrelevant sentences).
- [ ] Implement driver to run single-run and chained-run workflows, instrument tokens/latency/hits.
- [ ] Run small pilot (1000 requests) across small/med/large models, record baseline metrics.
- [ ] Run caching vs non-caching runs.
- [ ] Run sampling n variants (n=1 vs 3 vs 5) and compute cost per % improvement in accuracy.
- [ ] Draft quick dashboard in Console showing per-step breakdown and cost per completed response.

Questions / open design decisions:
- How to attribute cost to user-facing request when chaining causes multiple internal calls? Charge sum of tokens or pro-rate the extra internal cost? For internal experiments, show both.
- Should we surface a native "chain" abstraction in the API that declares steps and lets backend optimize (e.g., merge steps, keep shared prefix once)? Could expose hints: "share_prefix: true" so runtime can avoid repeat encoding.
- Can we do partial KV cache reuse across steps in the same request (i.e., keep encoder state in memory for short-lived chains)? That reduces recomputation but complicates autoscaling.

Notes to self (informal):
- talk to Maya about existing RLHF/verification setups — maybe reuse verification harness.
- Ethan has a small dashboard for prompt experiments; ask for permission to reuse panels.
- Keep storage of intermediate artifacts optional; privacy concern if intermediates contain PII. Add a flag redact_intermediates.

Potential API examples (sketch):
- naive: call A -> call B -> call C (3 separate requests)
- proposed: single POST /chains { steps: [ {prompt: ...}, {prompt_template: ... , share_prefix: true}, ... ], sampling: {n: 3}, verify: {...} } -> runtime can coalesce encodings and cache.

Quick idea: cost-aware chain optimizer (experimental)
- input: chain steps, per-step token estimates, quality delta estimates (from small pilot), latency SLOs
- output: recommended plan (merge steps, increase sampling only on verification step, pick model per-step).
- run as small local optimizer before sending to runtime (cheap heuristics).

Next steps (1-2 weeks):
- pilot run (1000) + preliminary dashboard + quick memo for SEs explaining tradeoffs.
- prototype chain-abstraction proposal for API (1 page).

Random scratch fragments (keep for personal context):
- metric to present to PM: $ per 1% precision improvement at 95% recall baseline.
- think about "step-sidecar" concept: short-lived local cache for a chain to avoid re-encoding long instruction templates multiple times.

End of file.
